# Getting help {#sec-getting-help}

**Core.** Work through it, with the exercises.

::: {.callout-note .goals icon=false}
## Learning goals

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

1. Look up how to use a tool with `--help`, `man`, and its official
   documentation, and read a usage line.
2. Read an error or warning: find which command printed it, what failed,
   and on what.
3. Work through a short checklist (message, log, location, environment,
   inputs, resources, recent changes) before asking for help.
4. Find the tools, versions, parameters, and reference reported in a
   paper's methods section, and say what the passage does not report.
5. Write a help request with the exact command, the complete message,
   versions, and a minimal example that still fails, with no passwords
   or private data, and check AI-suggested code before you run it.
:::

## What this chapter does {#sec-getting-help-intro}

Things break, for everyone, every day: a typo in a file name, a flag
that does not exist, a script run from the wrong folder, a download cut
short. Experienced people do not avoid errors; they get from a message
to a fix quickly, and they know when and how to ask. Most fixes take the
steps in this chapter, not expertise.

You will use the book's own files and environment throughout, so every
error in the chapter is one you can reproduce yourself, or read in the
captured output. You will finish able to:

- ask a tool how to use it (`--help`, `man`, its website);
- read an error message, and tell an error from a warning;
- work through a short checklist that solves most problems on its own;
- read a paper's methods section for tools, versions, and parameters;
- search well, and write a help request someone can answer;
- check a command an AI assistant suggests before you trust it.

Asking for help is part of the job, not a sign that you are not good
enough: some problems (a broken node, a full quota) only an
administrator can fix, and a clear request is a skill in its own right.

Commands run on your laptop, from the book's project folder,
`~/bioinf-computing` (@sec-organizing-projects). Practice files go in a
scratch folder, `~/bioinf-computing-ch04`, like Chapter 1's `~/bioinf-computing-ch01`, so
the project stays clean. Make it now:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch04
```

Cluster readers can run the same commands on a login node: they are
small and quick.

## Asking the tool itself: `--help`, `man`, docs {#sec-getting-help-docs}

Every tool you use can tell you how to use it. Start with seqkit, from
the book environment:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run seqkit --help
```

```{.console}
SeqKit -- a cross-platform and ultrafast toolkit for FASTA/Q file manipulation

Version: 2.14.0

Author: Wei Shen <shenwei356@gmail.com>

Documents  : http://bioinf.shenwei.me/seqkit
Source code: https://github.com/shenwei356/seqkit
Please cite: https://doi.org/10.1002/imt2.191
...
Usage:
  seqkit [command]

Commands for Basic Operation:
  faidx           create the FASTA index file and extract subsequences
  ...
  stats           simple statistics of FASTA/Q files
  ...
```

(`...` marks lines left out here; the real output is longer.) The top
already answers three questions you will have often: **which version**
you have (2.14.0), **where the documentation is**, and **what to cite**.
SeqKit's authors ask you to cite the SeqKit2 paper [@shen2024seqkit2].
Below that comes the list of **subcommands**: seqkit is one program with
many tools inside, and `stats`, which you ran in @sec-book-setup, is one
of them. Each subcommand has its own help:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run seqkit stats --help
```

Scroll to the `Flags:` part. Find the flag that prints a table for
other programs to read, and the one that sets how many CPUs seqkit uses:

```{.console}
  -T, --tabular              output in machine-friendly tabular format
  ...
  -j, --threads int                     number of CPUs. can also set with environment variable
                                        SEQKIT_THREADS) (default 4)
```

Now a tool that came with the system. On Linux and WSL, `gzip` is GNU
gzip; on a Mac it is the GNU gzip you installed in @sec-orientation:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gzip --help
```

```{.console}
Usage: gzip [OPTION]... [FILE]...
Compress or uncompress FILEs (by default, compress FILES in-place).

Mandatory arguments to long options are mandatory for short options too.

  -c, --stdout      write on standard output, keep original files unchanged
  -d, --decompress  decompress
  ...
  -t, --test        test compressed file integrity
  ...
With no FILE, or when FILE is -, read standard input.
```

Most command-line programs also have a **manual page**, a longer
description that opens in a pager:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
man gzip
```

Move with {{< kbd Space >}} and the arrow keys, search with `/` followed
by a word and {{< kbd Enter >}}, and quit with `q` (these are the keys of
`less`, @sec-shell-basics). Now try seqkit:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run man seqkit
```

```{.console}
No manual entry for seqkit
```

Many bioinformatics tools have no manual page, only `--help` and a
website. That is normal.

### Reading a usage line

Help text uses a compact notation, shown in @fig-usage-line.

::: {#fig-usage-line}
{{< svg ../figures/usage-line.svg >}}

How to read help text. In a usage line, square brackets mark something
optional, `...` means it may repeat, and capitals stand for something you
supply; you never type the brackets or dots. Flag lines give a short and
a long form of the same flag, a description, and, for flags that take a
value, the type of value.
:::

The conventions, from `Usage: gzip [OPTION]... [FILE]...`:

- **Square brackets** mark something optional. `[FILE]` means you may
  give a file; with none, gzip reads its input from elsewhere
  (@sec-text-tools).
- **`...`** means "may repeat": any number of options, any number of
  files.
- **Capitals**, or words in angle brackets such as `<file>`, commonly
  stand for a value you supply.
- **You never type the brackets or the dots.** `gzip -t reads.fastq.gz`,
  not `gzip [-t] [reads.fastq.gz]...`.

These are common conventions, not rules every tool follows, but most do.
Flags come in a **short form** (`-T`, one dash, one letter) and a **long
form** (`--tabular`, two dashes, a word); both mean the same, and the
long one is easier to read later. Some flags take a **value**: `-j 4` and
`--threads 4` both ask for four CPUs. Tools with subcommands, such as
`seqkit stats`, `samtools sort`, or `git commit`, have help at each
level. Not every tool answers `--help`: some use `-h`, some `help`, and
some print their usage when run with no arguments at all.

@tbl-help-sources lists where to look.

::: {.wide-table}
: Where to find out how a tool works. Only the ones that come from the
program you run are sure to match your installed version.
{#tbl-help-sources}

| Source | What it gives | Matches your installed version? | Example |
|:-------|:--------------|:--------------------------------|:--------|
| `--help` or `-h` | Usage line, flags, short descriptions | yes: the program prints it | `pixi run seqkit --help` |
| Subcommand help | The flags of one subcommand | yes | `pixi run seqkit stats --help` |
| `man` page | A longer manual, in a pager | usually; on a Mac, check (below) | `man gzip` |
| Official documentation site | Tutorials, examples, every option | the latest release, which may not be yours | [bioinf.shenwei.me/seqkit](https://bioinf.shenwei.me/seqkit/) |
| `--version` | The version you have | yes | `gzip --version`, `pixi run seqkit version` |
| R's `?` | The help page of an R function | yes | `?read.csv` (@sec-r-essentials) |
| Python's `help()` | The help of a Python function or module | yes | `help(open)` (@sec-python-essentials) |
:::

**Why the version matters.** A website describes the latest release;
your environment has the version in `pixi.lock`
(`pixi list` shows it, @sec-book-setup). If a flag from the website is
not in your `--help`, the website is probably ahead of your copy.

::: {.callout-tip}
## `--help` always matches what you run
`--help` is printed by the program you actually run, so it matches your
version. Online docs may describe a newer one, and on a Mac, `man` may
show the page of a different program with the same name.
:::

That last point is a macOS detail. After @sec-orientation's setup, `ls`
and `sed` run the GNU tools, and the `MANPATH` lines you added there make
`man ls` open the GNU page too. If a `man` page ever describes options
your command rejects, trust `--help`.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** In `Usage: gzip [OPTION]... [FILE]...`, must you give
a file?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
No. `[FILE]` is in square brackets, so it is optional; with no file,
gzip reads standard input, as the last line of its help says
(@sec-text-tools).
:::
:::

## Reading an error message {#sec-getting-help-errors}

**A diagnosis round first.** Below are six commands that fail, each run
on the book's files with its real output (captured with seqkit 2.14.0, R
4.4.3, and pixi {{< var pixi-version >}}). For each one, say what went
wrong before you open the answer. Two need a file you make first, a copy
of the first read file cut short:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
head -c 1000000 data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz > ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/broken.fastq.gz
```

(`head -c 1000000` keeps the first million bytes, under half the file.
It writes to the scratch folder, never into `data/raw/`.)

**1.**

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
seqkit stats data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
```

```{.console}
bash: seqkit: command not found
```

**2.**

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run seqkit stats data/raw/SRR6357070_l.fastq.gz
```

```{.console}
[ERRO] stat data/raw/SRR6357070_l.fastq.gz: no such file or directory
```

**3.**

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run seqkit stats –T data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
```

```{.console}
[ERRO] stat –T: no such file or directory
```

**4.**

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run seqkit stats --paired data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
```

```{.console}
Error: unknown flag: --paired
Usage:
  seqkit stats [flags]
...
unknown flag: --paired
```

**5.**

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run seqkit stats -T ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/broken.fastq.gz
```

```{.console}
[ERRO] /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch04/broken.fastq.gz: unexpected EOF
[ERRO]
file	format	type	num_seqs	sum_len	min_len	avg_len	max_len
```

**6.**

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run Rscript -e 'read.csv("data/meta/samples.csv")'
```

```{.console}
Error in file(file, "rt") : cannot open the connection
Calls: read.csv -> read.table -> file
In addition: Warning message:
In file(file, "rt") :
  cannot open file 'data/meta/samples.csv': No such file or directory
Execution halted
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answers

1. **`command not found`**, printed by the shell (`bash:`): no program
   called `seqkit` is on this shell's `PATH`, so it never started. The
   fix is `pixi run` (@sec-book-setup). If another copy of seqkit were
   installed somewhere else, the bare command would have run *that*
   copy instead, possibly a different version (@sec-linux-system).
2. **A typo.** The file name has a lowercase letter `l` where the digit
   `1` belongs: `_l.fastq.gz`. `ls data/raw/` shows the real names.
3. **An en dash.** `–T` starts with an en dash (`–`), not a hyphen
   (`-`). This happens when a command is copied from a PDF or a word
   processor. seqkit does not recognise it as a flag, so it treats `–T`
   as a file name and cannot find it. Retype the dash.
4. **A flag that does not exist.** seqkit stats has no `--paired`; it
   prints its usage to show what it does accept. (@sec-getting-help-ai
   comes back to where this flag came from.)
5. **A file cut short.** The `[ERRO]` line says `unexpected EOF`
   (end of file): the gzip data stops in the middle. seqkit still
   printed the table's header line, with no rows.
6. **The wrong file name.** The error says only *cannot open the
   connection*; the warning below it says which file and why: there is
   no `data/meta/samples.csv`. The file in @sec-organizing-projects is
   `samples.tsv`.
:::

### Who, what, and on what

You may have noticed a pattern. @fig-error-anatomy shows it on two of
the messages.

::: {#fig-error-anatomy}
{{< svg ../figures/error-anatomy.svg >}}

A reading strategy for error messages: find **who** printed it, **what**
failed, and **on what** (the file, flag, or object, often quoted). In
seqkit's message, `[ERRO]` is a severity label; you know seqkit printed
it because you ran seqkit. In R's, the function is named, and the file
is only in the warning that follows the error.
:::

- **Who** printed it. A message starting `bash:` comes from the shell:
  it could not even start the program. Otherwise it usually comes from
  the program you ran, which you know from your command. `[ERRO]`,
  `Error`, and `WARNING` are **severity labels**, not names. R's
  `Error in file(...)` names the function that failed.
- **What** failed: `stat` (looking a file up), `cannot open`, `unknown
  flag`, `unexpected EOF`.
- **On what**: the file, flag, or object, often in quotes. Read it
  character by character; that is where `_l` and `–T` were hiding.

Not every message has all three. A program that runs out of memory may
print only `Killed`; a crash may print almost nothing. Then the log and
the checklist (@sec-getting-help-checklist) carry the diagnosis.

**Read all of it.** Long messages are common, and the last line is not
always the one that matters. Look for the **earliest relevant failure
in this run**: later lines are often consequences of the first one. But
the useful detail can sit further down, as in R's message, where the
reason is in the warning *after* the error. And a log you append to may
still hold errors from earlier runs; check the times.

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
Look for who printed the message, what failed, and on what. Read all of
it, and find the earliest relevant failure in this run. An exit status
of 0 means "reported success", not "right answer".
:::

### Errors and warnings

An **error** reports that something failed. Whether the program or your
script then stops depends on the program and the script
(@sec-shell-scripts). A **warning** asks you to look: sometimes the
result is still what you wanted, sometimes not. In R:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run Rscript -e 'as.integer(c("12","7","n/a"))'
```

```{.console}
[1] 12  7 NA
Warning message:
NAs introduced by coercion
```

R turned `"n/a"` into `NA` (missing) and carried on. That is right if
`n/a` really means "missing" in that column, and wrong if it was a typo
for a number. Only you know which.

### Exit status

Every command, when it finishes, reports a number to the shell: its
**exit status**. `0` means the program reports success; anything else
means it reports a failure. `echo $?` prints the status of the command
just before it, so run it **immediately** after: any other command in
between replaces the number.

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
seqkit version
echo $?
```

```{.console}
bash: seqkit: command not found
127
```

`127` is the shell's code for "command not found". Now the truncated
file from round 5:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run seqkit stats -T ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/broken.fastq.gz
echo $?
```

```{.console}
[ERRO] /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch04/broken.fastq.gz: unexpected EOF
[ERRO]
file	format	type	num_seqs	sum_len	min_len	avg_len	max_len
0
```

seqkit 2.14.0 printed an error **and** reported success. (SeqKit's
current [documentation](https://bioinf.shenwei.me/seqkit/) says read
errors give a nonzero status, so a later version may behave
differently.) That is the lesson, whatever the version: the exit status
says what the program *reported*. It does not prove the output answers
your question. Read the messages, and check the result against
something you know: here, a table with no rows instead of 50,000 reads.
Given an intact file and this broken one in the same command, seqkit
2.14.0 printed only the header line: the intact file's row was lost too,
and the status was still `0`. How scripts and pipelines use exit status is @sec-shell-scripts.

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "If no error appears, the result is right"
**Reality.** Warnings let runs continue, and some tool versions report
success after printing an error (seqkit 2.14.0 on a truncated file).
Check outputs against something you know: a read count, a file size, a
number from the paper.
:::

@tbl-common-errors collects the messages you are most likely to meet in
the first part of this book.

::: {.wide-table}
: Common messages in Part I, and what to check first. {#tbl-common-errors}

| Message | Who prints it | Usual cause | First thing to check |
|:--------|:--------------|:------------|:---------------------|
| `command not found` | the shell | program not installed, or not on `PATH` | `pixi run` in front? the right folder? (@sec-linux-system) |
| `No such file or directory` | the shell or the program | wrong name or path, wrong folder | `pwd`, `ls`; spelling, `l` vs `1`, extension |
| `Permission denied` | the shell or the program | writing where you may not, such as read-only `data/raw/` | write somewhere else (@sec-organizing-projects) |
| `unknown flag`, `unrecognized option` | the program | flag does not exist in your version, or an en dash | `--help`; retype dashes |
| `unexpected EOF` | the program | file cut short (failed download or copy) | `gzip -t`, checksums (@sec-organizing-projects) |
| `No space left on device` | the program or the system | disk full | `df -h .` (@sec-orientation) |
| `Disk quota exceeded` | the system | your share of shared storage is full | your site's quota command (@sec-cluster-sites) |
| `Killed` | the shell | often, not always, out of memory | the scheduler's records (@sec-hpc-slurm) |
:::

Other languages have their own common messages (R's `could not find
function`, Python's `ModuleNotFoundError`); they come with
@sec-r-essentials and @sec-python-essentials.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** A message starts `bash: samtools: command not
found`. Did samtools run?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
No. The message comes from the shell (`bash:`), which could not find a
program called `samtools`, so it never started. Check whether you need
`pixi run` (or, on a cluster, `module load`).
:::
:::

## Before you ask: a troubleshooting checklist {#sec-getting-help-checklist}

Two cases first.

**Case 1: the wrong folder.** Go to your home folder and run Chapter
3's script, the way you ran it there:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~
pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh
```

```{.console}
Error:   × could not find pixi.toml or pyproject.toml with tool.pixi at directory /home/you
```

pixi looks for `pixi.toml` in the folder you are in (and the folders
above it) and finds none. (If some folder above yours held a
`pixi.toml`, the message would differ: pixi would use that one, and the
error would come later.) The fix is the folder, not the command:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pwd
cd ~/bioinf-computing
```

**Case 2: a pattern that matches nothing.**

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fq.gz
```

```{.console}
[ERRO] stat data/raw/*.fq.gz: no such file or directory
```

The clue is the `*` inside the message. bash replaces a pattern such as
`*.fq.gz` with the matching file names, but when nothing matches it
passes the pattern on unchanged, and seqkit looks for a file literally
called `*.fq.gz`. `ls data/raw/` shows the files end in `.fastq.gz`, not
`.fq.gz`. Why bash does this is @sec-shell-basics.

Both cases are solved by a question you can ask of almost any problem.
@fig-troubleshooting-checklist puts those questions in order.

::: {#fig-troubleshooting-checklist}
{{< svg ../figures/troubleshooting-checklist.svg >}}

A troubleshooting checklist. Each step has an exit: stop as soon as the
problem is solved. The wrong-folder case stops at step 3, the `*.fq.gz`
case at step 4. Still stuck after step 7? Leave the checklist and ask.
:::

1. **Read the message**, all of it (@sec-getting-help-errors).
2. **Find the log.** The terminal may show only the last lines; a log
   can hold the first error. More below.
3. **Where am I, with what?** `pwd`, `hostname`, `ls`; did you use
   `pixi run`? On a cluster, which modules are loaded?
4. **Do the inputs exist and look right?** `ls -l`, `head`, `gzip -t`,
   `md5sum -c` (@sec-organizing-projects); do the names in your sample
   sheet match the file names?
5. **Are resources short?** `No space left on device`, `Disk quota
   exceeded`, a time limit, `Killed` (@tbl-resource-limits).
6. **What changed** since it last worked? New data, a new version, a new
   folder, a new machine?
7. **Make it small.** Does it still fail on 100 reads, on one sample?
   (@sec-getting-help-asking shows how.)

Not every step is needed every time; stop when it is solved. If it is
still not solved after step 7, the way out is to **ask**
(@sec-getting-help-search, @sec-getting-help-asking), with what you
checked.

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
Most problems are found by the same few questions: where am I, with
which software, on which inputs, with enough resources, and what
changed. Stop when it is solved.
:::

**Finding the log.** Chapter 3's script writes a log in `logs/` every
time it runs, one file per run, with everything it printed. Here is the
log of a run that failed because a raw file had been moved out of
`data/raw/` (captured; the host name is replaced):

```{.default filename="logs/01_count_reads_2026-11-17T122821_jlSC.log"}
started:  2026-11-17 12:28:21 -0600
host:     <laptop>
script:   76fa8eb6a7b90f212042cfbe6d95cfcc  src/01_count_reads.sh
seqkit:   seqkit v2.14.0
checking inputs against data/raw/checksums.md5:
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: OK
md5sum: SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: No such file or directory
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: FAILED open or read
md5sum: WARNING: 1 listed file could not be read
```

No `finished:` line, so the run stopped early. The earliest relevant
failure is the line naming `SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz`: who (`md5sum`), what
(could not open it), on what (the R2 file). The run never reached
`seqkit stats`, so `results/` still holds the *previous* run's counts:
another reason to check the log, not only whether a results file exists.
The log keeps all this after the terminal is closed, with the date, the
machine, and the versions.

Not every program writes a log, and a log does not always name the
cause. Later chapters add more places to look: a cluster job's output
file, `slurm-<jobid>.out` (@sec-hpc-slurm), and a pipeline's
`.nextflow.log` and each task's `.command.err` (@sec-nf-core). On a
cluster, steps 3 and 5 matter more: which node you are on, which
modules are loaded, and which quota is full.

**When to ask.** If you have made no progress for about an hour, that
is a good point to stop and ask; your lab's habits come first, and it is
not a limit you must reach. Ask **at once** for anything about accounts,
passwords, or keys; when a fix could damage data or affect other users;
and when something that worked stops working in a way your own changes
do not explain (a slow or missing filesystem, a module that will not
load, a quota). You do not need to know whether the system is at fault:
report what you saw and what you checked.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: changing many things at once
Change one thing, rerun, and look. Three changes at once leave you not
knowing which one fixed the problem, or which one broke something else.
:::

@tbl-checklist is the same checklist as a table, with the chapter that
goes deeper on each step.

: The troubleshooting checklist. {#tbl-checklist}

| Step | Question | Commands or places to look | Goes deeper |
|:-----|:---------|:---------------------------|:------------|
| 1 | What does the message say? | who, what, on what; the earliest relevant failure | this chapter |
| 2 | Where is the log? | the terminal; `logs/`; `slurm-<jobid>.out`; `.nextflow.log` | @sec-organizing-projects, @sec-hpc-slurm, @sec-nf-core |
| 3 | Where am I, with what? | `pwd`, `hostname`, `ls`, `pixi run`, `module list` | @sec-linux-system |
| 4 | Do the inputs exist and look right? | `ls -l`, `head`, `gzip -t`, `md5sum -c` | @sec-organizing-projects, @sec-fasta-fastq |
| 5 | Are resources short? | `df -h .`, quota commands, job records | @sec-orientation, @sec-hpc-slurm |
| 6 | What changed? | `NOTEBOOK.md`, `pixi.lock`, dates in `logs/` | @sec-git |
| 7 | Does it fail when small? | 100 reads, one sample | @sec-getting-help-asking |

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** A script worked yesterday and fails today with `No
such file or directory`. Name two checklist questions to ask first.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Where am I (`pwd`)? Do the inputs exist (`ls -l`)? And what changed: a
moved folder, a renamed file?
:::
:::

## Reading a methods section {#sec-getting-help-methods}

When you want to repeat or build on an analysis, the paper's methods
section is where you find out which tools, versions, and parameters
were used. The book's running dataset comes from @wu2018repression,
which is openly licensed (CC BY), so it can be quoted here. Open it in
[PubMed Central](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6310685/) and
find two places: the *Software and Algorithms* rows of the **Key
Resources Table**, and the paragraph *Differential Expression Analysis*
in the methods.

Four words you will meet there, one line each (the Transcriptomics book
explains them):

- **Adapter trimming**: cutting the sequencing adapters off the ends of
  reads.
- **Alignment**: finding where in the genome each read comes from.
- **Counting**: how many reads fall in each gene.
- **Differential expression**: which genes change between conditions.

**Your turn.** Fill in @tbl-methods-extract for the RNA-seq analysis
from those two places, before you open the answer. The last two
columns matter: what the paper *prints*, and what you would *type*.

: What the methods of @wu2018repression report for the RNA-seq analysis.
"As printed" keeps the paper's typography, spaces included; see the
discoveries below.
{#tbl-methods-extract}

| Step | Tool | Version | Parameters as printed | As you would type them | Reference, data |
|:-----|:-----|:--------|:----------------------|:-----------------------|:----------------|
| Trim adapters | ? | ? | ? | ? | — |
| Align and quantify | ? | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| Differential expression | ? | ? | ? | ? | — |

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

| Step | Tool | Version | Parameters as printed | As you would type them | Reference, data |
|:-----|:-----|:--------|:----------------------|:-----------------------|:----------------|
| Trim adapters | cutadapt | 1.9.1 | `–minimum-length=25–quality-cutoff=20 -a AGATCGGAAGAGC -A AGATCGGAAGAGC` | `--minimum-length=25 --quality-cutoff=20 -a AGATCGGAAGAGC -A AGATCGGAAGAGC` | — |
| Align and quantify | RSEM with STAR | 1.3.0; STAR 2.5.2a | `–star-output-genome-bam–forward-prob 0`, all else default | `--star-output-genome-bam --forward-prob 0` | *S. cerevisiae* genes from Ensembl, assembly R64-1-1, release 90 |
| Differential expression | DESeq2 | 1.12.3, in R 3.3.1 | not reported in this excerpt | — | — |
:::

Three things to notice.

**The dashes and the spaces.** The paper prints `–minimum-length` and
`–forward-prob` with a single en dash: typesetting turned the two
hyphens of `--` into one `–`. Copied as printed, they fail exactly like
round 3 of @sec-getting-help-errors. Look again at the spacing, too:
`–minimum-length=25–quality-cutoff=20` and
`–star-output-genome-bam–forward-prob` have no space between the two
options, so a program would read each pair as one long, unknown word.
Both faults need repairing before the command can run.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: commands copied from PDFs and web pages
Typesetting turns `--` into `–` and straight quotes (`"`, `'`) into
curly ones (`“`, `’`). The command looks right and fails, or worse, does
something else. Retype dashes and quotes when you copy from a paper.
:::

**The strandedness setting.** `--forward-prob 0` says how the library
was made: which strand of the gene each read comes from (@sec-nf-core and
the Transcriptomics book explain strandedness). The nf-core test sheet
the book uses (@sec-organizing-projects) says `auto` for our sample,
`WT_REP1`. `auto` asks the pipeline to *work out* the strandedness from
the reads; it does not state it, so it is not a second source for the
paper's value.

**What this excerpt does not report.** The STAR and RSEM index settings,
DESeq2's design and thresholds, and any code. Before saying the paper
*omits* them, check its supplements and any deposited code. A complete
methods section names the tool, the version, the parameters, the
reference release, and where the code and data are: the same chain you
recorded for your own project in @sec-organizing-projects.

Two cautions. First, the book later runs these reads through
nf-core/rnaseq (@sec-nf-core). That is a different, newer analysis, not
a reconstruction of the paper's. Second, a methods section can describe
several kinds of library: this paper also has single-end TSS-seq reads
of 76 bases. Which paragraph describes *our* reads? Exercise 4 checks it
against the run's public record.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** The excerpt says "STAR (version 2.5.2a)" but not
the index options. Can you reproduce the alignment exactly from the
excerpt?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Not for certain: index settings can change the results. Check the
supplements and any deposited code; then either assume the defaults
(and say so) or ask the authors.
:::
:::

## Searching, and choosing where to ask {#sec-getting-help-search}

Most errors have been seen before. Searching well means turning *your*
message into one that matches other people's. Take this one, from a
truncated file on a cluster:

```{.console}
[ERRO] /home/<user>/proj/sample_17_R1.fq.gz: unexpected EOF
```

Remove what is yours (the path, the sample name), keep the distinctive
part in quotes, and add the tool's name:

```{.default}
seqkit "unexpected EOF"
```

Search the tool's own GitHub issues too, for example
[seqkit's](https://github.com/shenwei356/seqkit/issues), **including
closed ones**: a closed issue often holds the answer. Reading issues is
all you need here; filing one is @sec-github.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Search tip
Search the distinctive part of the message in quotes, without your
paths and sample names, plus the tool's name.
:::

**Where to ask** depends on the kind of problem (@tbl-where-to-ask).
If your lab has local experts and asks them first, do that.

::: {.wide-table}
: Where to ask, by kind of problem. {#tbl-where-to-ask}

| Kind of problem | Where to ask | Who answers | Before posting |
|:----------------|:-------------|:------------|:---------------|
| Account, password, quota, node, module, anything about one cluster | your cluster's help desk: [SCINet's VRSC](https://scinet.usda.gov/support/contact), [ISU Research IT](https://research.it.iastate.edu/contact-us) for Nova, or your own site's (@sec-cluster-sites) | the site's staff | say which cluster, node, and job |
| How to use a Bioconductor package | [Bioconductor support site](https://support.bioconductor.org) | package authors and users | read its [posting guide](https://bioconductor.org/help/support/posting-guide/); include `sessionInfo()` |
| An nf-core pipeline | [nf-core's channels](https://nf-co.re/join) (@sec-nf-core) | pipeline developers and users | the pipeline version and command |
| Another tool | its documentation, then its GitHub issues or discussions | the tool's authors | search closed issues first |
| A general bioinformatics question | [Biostars](https://www.biostars.org) | other bioinformaticians | search first |
| General R, Python, or shell | [Stack Overflow](https://stackoverflow.com) | programmers | a [minimal reproducible example](https://stackoverflow.com/help/minimal-reproducible-example) |
| A command from this book | the book's [**Report an issue!**](../reporting.qmd) page | the author | the *Something doesn't run* form |
:::

**Judging an answer.** How old is it, and which version does it assume?
Is it from the tool's authors or documentation? Does it explain *why*?
And does it work on your small example? A 2015 answer may name flags
that no longer exist.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** Your job on the cluster cannot write to `/project`,
and the quota command shows you at your limit. Where do you ask?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Your cluster's help desk, or your PI if the project's quota is theirs to
raise. Not Biostars: nobody there can change your quota.
:::
:::

## Asking for help {#sec-getting-help-asking}

Here is a request that is hard to answer:

> seqkit doesn't work on the cluster, help!!
>
> *[a screenshot of the last few lines of a terminal]*

A helper cannot tell which command, which files, which version, or even
which error: the screenshot cuts off the first line. They have to ask
four questions before they can start. @fig-good-request shows the same
problem written so that someone can answer at once.

::: {#fig-good-request}
{{< svg ../figures/good-request.svg >}}

A help request someone can answer. It starts from the book's *Something
doesn't run* form (where it ran, the exact command, the complete message
as text, `pixi info`) and adds what a question about a tool needs: what
you wanted and expected, what you tried, the tool's version, and a small
example. Private details become placeholders that keep the fault
visible.
:::

The book's own [*Something doesn't run*](../reporting.qmd) form is a
good starting model: **where it ran** (laptop, login node, or compute
node; operating system; cluster), the **exact command**, copied, the
**complete message as text**, and `pixi info`. A question about a tool
also needs:

- **what you were trying to do**, and what you expected;
- **what you tried** already;
- **the failing tool's version**;
- **a small example** that still fails.

**Versions, each for its own question.**

- `pixi info` describes where and how: the platform, pixi's version, the
  environment, and its folders. It does **not** list package versions.
- `pixi run seqkit version` gives the version of the tool that failed.
  With `pixi run`, it reports the copy that actually ran.
- `pixi list` shows every package's version, when several might matter.
- In R, `pixi run Rscript -e 'sessionInfo()'` (@sec-r-essentials).

Do not paste the whole `pixi.lock`; it is thousands of lines.

### A minimal reproducible example

A **minimal reproducible example** is the smallest input and the
shortest command that still show the problem. Shrink until it still
fails, and **rerun after every cut, to check that it still fails the
same way**. Fewer files, one sample, the first 100 reads:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run seqkit head -n 100 data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz \
  -o ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/small_R1.fastq.gz
```

That writes the first 100 reads (10,100 bases) to the scratch folder,
never to `data/raw/`. Now the catch. Do the same with the truncated
file, and check the small copy:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run seqkit head -n 100 ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/broken.fastq.gz \
  -o ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/small_broken.fastq.gz
pixi run seqkit stats -T ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/small_broken.fastq.gz
```

```{.console}
file	format	type	num_seqs	sum_len	min_len	avg_len	max_len
/home/you/bioinf-computing-ch04/small_broken.fastq.gz	FASTQ	DNA	100	10100	101	101.0	101
```

No error. The first 100 reads of the broken file are intact; the damage
is at its end. Shrinking removed the bug: this example is too small.
That is why you rerun after every cut. Some failures need no real data
at all (a wrong file name fails on any file), and often the shrinking
finds the bug for you. In R, the `reprex` package builds such examples
([reprex.tidyverse.org](https://reprex.tidyverse.org), @sec-r-essentials).

### Text, not screenshots

Paste commands and messages as **text**. Text can be searched, copied,
quoted, and read by screen readers; a screenshot can do none of these,
and it usually cuts off the first error. Put it in a Markdown code block,
between lines of three backticks (Markdown, @sec-organizing-projects):

````{.default}
```
Error: unknown flag: --paired
```
````

A screenshot can **add** to the text when the problem is something on
screen, such as a VS Code panel or a dialog. For a long log, post the
relevant part with a few lines around it, and keep the full log to
share if the venue asks for it.

### Privacy and etiquette

Before you post, replace user names, paths, and host names you would
rather not share with placeholders, and do it consistently (always
`<home>`, always `<user>`). Keep the fault visible while you do: the
relative layout, the extension, upper and lower case, the `l` vs `1`,
the en dash. `pixi info`, for example, prints paths in your home folder.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: secrets in public
Never post passwords, SSH private keys, tokens, unpublished data, or
data under a use agreement (ask your PI if unsure). Forums and issue
trackers are public, and what you post is copied and indexed: deleting
it later does not take it back.
:::

Two habits of good askers: if you post the same question in two
places, say so in each; and when it is solved, post the answer and mark
it solved, for the next person who searches.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** Why paste the error as text rather than a
screenshot?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Text can be searched, copied into a search engine, quoted in a reply,
and read by screen readers. Screenshots often cut off the first error,
and they hide the command.
:::
:::

@tbl-request-checklist sums up what goes into a request.

::: {.wide-table}
: What a help request includes, and what it never includes.
{#tbl-request-checklist}

| Include | Example | Why | Never include |
|:--------|:--------|:----|:--------------|
| Where it ran | laptop, macOS 15; or Nova, compute node | systems behave differently | host names you were asked not to share |
| What you wanted and expected | "count read pairs; one number per sample" | helpers can spot a wrong approach | — |
| The exact command | copied from the terminal | the fault may be one character | passwords typed on the command line |
| The complete message, as text | from the first relevant line | searchable, quotable | — |
| What you tried | "`--help` has no `--paired`" | saves repeating it | — |
| Versions | `pixi run seqkit version`; `pixi info` | behaviour changes between versions | your home path (use `<home>`) |
| A small example | 100 reads that still fail | others can reproduce it | unpublished or restricted data |
:::

## AI coding assistants {#sec-getting-help-ai}

AI coding assistants can explain an error, suggest a command, or draft a
help request. They can also be confidently wrong. Here is an answer to
"count read pairs in my paired FASTQ files with seqkit". It was written
for this book to show a typical mistake, not captured from a particular
assistant:

> Use seqkit's stats command with the `--paired` flag:
>
> ```
> seqkit stats --paired data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
> ```

Check it, in three steps:

1. **Is the flag real?** `pixi run seqkit stats --help` lists no
   `--paired`.
2. **Run it.** You did, in round 4 of @sec-getting-help-errors:
   `Error: unknown flag: --paired`.
3. **Fix it, then check what the answer means.** Without the invented
   flag, the command runs:

   ```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
   pixi run seqkit stats data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
   ```

   It prints one row per file, each with 50,000 reads. The two files are
   the two mates of the same fragments (@sec-orientation), so the run
   has **50,000 read pairs**, not 100,000. A command that runs is not
   yet an answer to the question.

**Rules for using an assistant:**

- Treat its suggestions as coming from a fast, confident colleague who
  is sometimes wrong.
- Check every flag against `--help` for **your** version.
- Test on small data with a known answer before real data.
- Understand any command before you run it, above all ones that delete
  or overwrite (`rm`, `>`, `mv`). Never run those unread on raw data or
  on shared systems.
- Paste error text and small toy examples. Never paste credentials,
  private or unpublished data, or anything your institution's or your
  data agreement's current policy restricts.
- Follow your journal's and your university's rules on disclosing AI
  use.

Used this way, assistants are good at the two skills this chapter
teaches: explaining an error message, and drafting a help request. As
long as you check the result.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: trusting an AI-suggested flag
Check every flag against `--help`, and test on data with a known
answer, before you run an AI-suggested command on real data.
:::

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "Code from an AI assistant works; I can assume it has been tested"
**Reality.** It is generated text. Flags can be invented or belong to
another version, and even code described as tested may have been tested
on other inputs or another system. Check flags in `--help` and reproduce
a known result.
:::

@tbl-ai-checks lists the checks.

: Checks for an AI-suggested command. {#tbl-ai-checks}

| Check | How | What it catches |
|:------|:----|:----------------|
| The flag exists | `--help` for your version | invented flags, flags from other tools |
| The version matches | `pixi run <tool> version`, `pixi list` | flags from a newer or older release |
| It works on toy data | 100 reads with a known answer | wrong output that looks plausible |
| The output means what you asked | compare with what you know (reads vs pairs) | an answer to a different question |
| Nothing is destroyed | read every `rm`, `>`, `mv` before running | lost or overwritten data |
| Nothing private is sent | paste only the question and toy examples | leaked data and credentials |

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** An assistant suggests `pixi run seqkit stats
--count-pairs data/raw/*.fastq.gz`. What do you check before trusting
it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
That `--count-pairs` appears in `pixi run seqkit stats --help` for your
version. It does not in seqkit 2.14.0: running it gives `Error: unknown
flag: --count-pairs`.
:::
:::

## Summary {#sec-getting-help-summary}

- `--help` comes from the program you run, so it matches your version;
  `man` pages and websites may not. In a usage line, brackets mean
  optional, `...` means repeatable, and you type neither.
- Read the whole message for who printed it, what failed, and on what,
  and find the earliest relevant failure. An exit status of 0 means the
  program reported success, not that the result is right.
- Before asking, work through the checklist: message, log, where and
  with what, inputs, resources, what changed, a small example. Stop as
  soon as it is solved.
- A methods section should give tool, version, parameters, and
  reference; retype its dashes, and say "not reported in this excerpt"
  until you have checked the supplements.
- A good help request has the exact command, the complete message as
  text, versions, and a small example that still fails, with nothing
  private in it. Check every AI-suggested flag in `--help` and test on
  data with a known answer.

## Exercises {#sec-getting-help-exercises}

::: {.check}
**Exercise 1. Fix a broken script.** Make the script below in the
scratch folder (in VS Code: `code ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/count.sh`, paste, save).
Copy it from this page exactly, faults and all:

```{.bash filename="~/bioinf-computing-ch04/count.sh"}
# count.sh: count reads in both raw files (has three faults)
# Run from ~/bioinf-computing:  pixi run bash ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/count.sh
seqkit stats –T --paired data/raw/SRR6357070_l.fastq.gz data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
```

From `~/bioinf-computing`, run it with `pixi run bash ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/count.sh`.
It fails three times. Fix one fault at a time, using only the message
and `--help`, and rerun after each fix. Note in `NOTEBOOK.md`
(@sec-organizing-projects) what each message said and what you changed.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
seqkit checks its flags before it looks at files, so the faults appear
in this order (exit status in brackets):

1. `Error: unknown flag: --paired`, followed by the usage [255]. Delete
   `--paired`.
2. `[ERRO] stat –T: no such file or directory` [255]. The en dash made
   `–T` a file name; retype it as `-T`.
3. `[ERRO] stat data/raw/SRR6357070_l.fastq.gz: no such file or
   directory` [255]. Change the letter `l` to the digit `1`.

The fixed line is
`seqkit stats -T data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz`,
and it prints [0]:

```{.console}
file	format	type	num_seqs	sum_len	min_len	avg_len	max_len
data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz	FASTQ	DNA	50000	5050000	101	101.0	101
data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz	FASTQ	DNA	50000	5050000	101	101.0	101
```

With several files, seqkit may also show a `processed files: 2 / 2`
progress line; it is not an error.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 2. Read the help.** From `pixi run seqkit stats --help`, find
the flag that adds quartiles and N50. Run `pixi run seqkit stats` with
that flag and `-T` on both raw files. Which columns appear that were not
there before? Do the two files differ in any of them?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`-a, --all`. The command is
`pixi run seqkit stats -a -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz`. The new columns are
`Q1`, `Q2`, `Q3` (quartiles of read length), `sum_gap`, `N50`,
`N50_num`, `Q20(%)`, `Q30(%)`, `AvgQual`, `GC(%)`, and `sum_n`. With
every read 101 bases long, the length columns are all 101. The quality
columns differ: R1 has `Q30(%)` 92 and `AvgQual` 26.89, R2 90 and
23.28; R2 also has far more `N` bases (`sum_n` 18,842 vs 280). Read 2
being a little worse is common in Illumina data (@sec-fasta-fastq).
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 3. Write a help request.** Pretend that exercise 1's first
error is one you cannot solve. Write the request in
`~/bioinf-computing-ch04/help_request.md`, following @fig-good-request: the
*Something doesn't run* fields (where it ran, the exact command, the
complete message as text, `pixi info` with your home path replaced by
`<home>`), plus what you expected, what you tried, the output of
`pixi run seqkit version`, and a small example. For the example, make a
100-read file with the `seqkit head` command from
@sec-getting-help-asking, and **check that the same error still appears
with it**. Then shrink once more: does the error need an input file at
all? Do not submit the request. Then test it: could someone reproduce
the failure from the request alone, without access to your home folder?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
The 100-read file gives the same `unknown flag` error, so the example
works. But one more cut shows it is not needed: the error appears with
no input file at all, because seqkit rejects the flag before it looks
for files:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run seqkit stats --paired
echo $?
```

```{.console}
Error: unknown flag: --paired
Usage:
  seqkit stats [flags]
...
unknown flag: --paired
255
```

So the smallest example is the command alone. A model request:

````{.default}
**seqkit stats: `unknown flag: --paired` when counting read pairs**

Where it ran: laptop, macOS 15 (Intel); no cluster.

Trying to: count read pairs in two mate files; expected one number.

Command (copied, run from the book's project folder):
```
pixi run seqkit stats --paired
```
No input file is needed: the same error appears with or without one.

Message (abbreviated here; the full output, with the usage and
flag list, is attached as error.txt):
```
Error: unknown flag: --paired
Usage:
  seqkit stats [flags]
...
unknown flag: --paired
```
Exit status: 255.

Tried: `pixi run seqkit stats --help` lists no `--paired`.

Versions: seqkit v2.14.0 (`pixi run seqkit version`), installed from
the book environment (pixi.toml and pixi.lock from Chapter 2 of
Computing for Bioinformatics). `pixi info`: Platform osx-64.
````

The test: yes, someone could reproduce it, because it needs only
seqkit 2.14.0 and one command, with no data, and the request says where
the environment comes from. Two things made the first draft fail the
test: a message cut with `...` but called complete, and a file name
(`small_R1.fastq.gz`) that a helper does not have. The fact most often
left out is the **tool's version** (`pixi info` does not show it); a
helper's first reply would be to ask for it.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 4. Match the paper to the data.** Open the ENA record for
the book's run,
[SRR6357070](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/browser/view/SRR6357070). Find
the library layout, the instrument, and the read count, and say what
unit the read count is in. Which methods paragraph of
@wu2018repression describes this run: the RNA-seq one, or the TSS-seq
one?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Recorded 2026-11-17, in case the page changes: sample GSM2879618,
"Wild-type total RNA-Seq biological replicate 1"; layout `PAIRED`;
Illumina HiSeq 2500; `read_count` 47,629,288; `base_count`
9,621,116,176. For a paired run, ENA's read count is in **read pairs**:
9,621,116,176 bases ÷ 47,629,288 = 202 bases per pair, which is
101 + 101.

It is the **RNA-seq** paragraph: about 45 million 101-base,
strand-specific, paired-end reads on a HiSeq 2500 or 4000. The TSS-seq
reads were 76 bases, single-end, on a HiSeq 4000. Our files are a
50,000-pair subset made by nf-core, so ENA's checksums are for the full
files, not ours (@sec-reference-data).
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 5. Check an AI answer.** Take the assistant's answer from
@sec-getting-help-ai, or, if you already use an AI assistant, ask it for
a seqkit command that counts read pairs in `data/raw/`. Check every flag
in `--help`, run the command, and say whether the output answers the
question: pairs, not reads. Record in `NOTEBOOK.md` what you checked. If
you use an assistant, paste only the question, no files.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
The book's answer fails at the first check (`--paired` is not in
`--help`) and at the second (`unknown flag`). Without the flag, seqkit
prints one row per mate file, 50,000 reads each, so the run has 50,000
pairs. An answer that adds the two `num_seqs` and reports 100,000 pairs
has run correctly and still answered the wrong question. Another
assistant may suggest something else; the checks are the same.
:::
:::

## Further reading {#sec-getting-help-reading}

- @dallolio2011ten --- written by people from Biostars and other
  bioinformatics forums: how to ask so that strangers want to answer.
- @haller2022ten --- what makes a bug report fixable, from a tool
  developer's side; useful now, and again when you file issues in
  @sec-github.
- @auslander2026ten --- rules for using AI assistants in computational
  biology, among them owning every line of generated code and using
  chatbots to recall syntax, not scientific reasoning.
- @stackoverflow2026minimal, [*How to create a Minimal, Reproducible
  Example*](https://stackoverflow.com/help/minimal-reproducible-example)
  --- one short page on shrinking a problem until someone else can run
  it.
